summary.text: Public-key cryptography, also called asymmetric cryptography, uses pairs of related keys: a public key that can be shared openly and a private key kept secret.
Anyone can encrypt with the public key, but only the holder of the private key can decrypt, so no secret key has to be exchanged in advance.
Because it can be slow, protocols such as TLS, SSH and PGP combine it with faster symmetric cryptography in hybrid systems.

facts.value: One public key and one matching private key

facts.value: Sign with the private key, verify with the public key

items.prompt: A computer receives a software update. How can it confirm the update really comes from the publisher?

options.label: Decrypt the update using the publisher's private key
Trust any update that arrives over the internet
Ask the publisher to email the private key
Verify its signature using the publisher's public key

items.explain: The publisher signs updates with the private key, and any computer can verify the signature with the public key. A forger without the private key cannot pass verification.

items.prompt: Sources email secret messages to a journalist who posted a key on a website, and an eavesdropper reads the email in transit. Who can read the messages?

options.label: Only the journalist, who holds the matching private key
Anyone who has seen the posted key
The eavesdropper, since the email passes through them
Nobody, not even the journalist

items.explain: Anyone with the public key can encrypt, but only those who know the corresponding private key can decrypt the ciphertexts.

items.prompt: A company with many employees wants every pair to talk privately using one shared secret key per conversation. What problem does it run into?

options.label: Each secret key can only be used once per day
Every pair needs a separate key, which becomes unmanageable as people join
Secret keys cannot be written down or stored anywhere
Employees would all end up able to read each other's mail

items.explain: With only shared-key systems, a separate key is required for each possible pair of users, which quickly becomes unmanageable as participants increase.

items.prompt: Why do systems like TLS and SSH use public-key methods only to set up a shared key, then switch to another kind of encryption?

options.label: Public-key methods cannot be used to hide a message at all
Shared-key methods are always more secure in every respect
Public-key methods are much more computationally intensive than shared-key ones
Public keys expire after a single use

items.explain: Asymmetric algorithms are nearly always much more computationally intensive than symmetric ones, so they are used to exchange a symmetric key that does the bulk of the work.

items.prompt: Bob receives a message encrypted with his public key. What does the encryption by itself tell him about who sent it?

options.label: It proves the sender is a trusted friend
It reveals the sender's private key
It shows the sender is the key's owner
Nothing, since it only conceals the content

items.explain: Anyone can use a public key, so encryption alone conceals the content but says nothing about who sent the message.

items.prompt: Mia generates a key pair and wants her messages to stay safe. Which way of handling the two keys keeps security intact?

options.label: Share the public key widely and keep the private key to herself
Keep both keys secret from everyone, including friends
Share the private key and keep the public key hidden
Post both keys so anyone can check them

items.explain: Security depends on keeping the private key secret, while the public key can be openly distributed without compromising security.

paragraphs.heading: Two keys instead of one
paragraphs.text: Public-key cryptography, also called asymmetric cryptography, uses pairs of related keys. Each pair has a public key and a matching private key. The pairs are made by algorithms built on mathematical problems known as one-way functions. The whole system stays safe as long as the private key is kept secret, while the public key can be handed out to anyone.

paragraphs.heading: The problem it solves
paragraphs.text: Until the mid-1970s, every cipher was symmetric: sender and receiver used the same key and both had to keep it secret. That key had to travel between them safely before any message could be sent, for example over a secure channel. This gets out of hand quickly as more people join, when no secure channel exists, or when keys are changed often. Keeping messages private from other users even needs a separate key for every possible pair of people. With public keys, only the private halves must stay hidden, and the public halves can be spread widely.

paragraphs.heading: Signing with a private key
paragraphs.text: In a digital signature system, a sender combines a private key with a message to make a signature. Anyone holding the matching public key can check whether the signature fits the message, but a forger without the private key cannot produce a message and signature that pass. A software maker, for instance, can build its public key into its programs. Later updates signed with the private key can then be checked by every computer, and fake updates from a forger will not be accepted.

paragraphs.heading: Locking with a public key
paragraphs.text: In a public-key encryption system, anyone with the public key can lock a message, but only the holder of the private key can open it again. A journalist could post a public key on a website so that sources can send scrambled messages that only the journalist can read, even if someone intercepts the email. This does not hide the surrounding details, such as which computer sent a message, when, or how long it is. Nor does it tell the receiver who the sender was; it only hides the content.

paragraphs.heading: Mixing fast and slow
paragraphs.text: Asymmetric methods nearly always take much more computing than symmetric ones, and can be too slow for many tasks. So a common pattern is to use the public-key method only to pass along a symmetric key, then send the actual data with that shared key. PGP, SSH and the SSL/TLS family work this way and are called hybrid cryptosystems. Nobody has to deliver a key by hand beforehand, on paper or by courier, yet the bulk of the traffic gets the speed of symmetric encryption.

paragraphs.heading: Where it can fail
paragraphs.text: The chief danger is that a private key becomes known, at which point all the security that relied on it is gone. Recent TLS schemes reduce this risk with forward secrecy, which creates short-lived keys during a conversation that an attacker would also need. Any public-key scheme can in theory be cracked by trying every key, but not if the computing required, which Claude Shannon called the work factor, is beyond every attacker; often a longer key raises it. Quantum computing makes many of these algorithms vulnerable, and quantum-resistant replacements are being developed.
